title: The Baker Reversal: Alex Takes the Trophy, Jon Takes the Spoon
title_candidates: The Baker Reversal: Alex Takes the Trophy, Jon Takes the Spoon
Three Spoons and a Trophy: Alex Baker's Turn at Camiral
Won on Day One: Alex Baker Leads TEG 18 From the Fifth Hole
theme: TEG 18 turned the established order on its head. The Baker with three Wooden Spoons to his name won the Trophy; the Baker who won both Trophy and Jacket at TEG 17 finished bottom, 43 points behind his own brother; and last year's Spoon holder, Gregg Williams, walked off with the Green Jacket. Underneath the reversal sits an unglamorous mechanism: Alex Baker built the whole margin, and more, in the first eighteen holes, and then simply refused to go away.
opening_hook: Open on the final Stadium scoreboard after R4, with the two Baker names at opposite ends of the same column — Alex on 169 and the Trophy, Jon on 126 and the Spoon — then rewind twelve months to Jon holding both Trophy and Jacket at TEG 17. The reversal is the hook; the four rounds are the explanation.

trophy_storyline.subject: How Alex Baker, owner of three prior Wooden Spoons, led the Trophy from the fifth hole of round one to the last and won by eight
trophy_storyline.why_it_matters: The Trophy is the main event, and this one was effectively over by Saturday teatime: a 46 in R1 opened a twelve-point gap on John Patterson that three days of scrapping never closed.
trophy_storyline.shape: Setup: Baker takes the lead at the 5th in R1 and posts 46 — best in the field — built on 17 points across holes 8-12 (b40) and 13 more across 14-16 (b47), and leads by twelve. Turn: R2 on the Tour course is a mess — an 8 at the 16th, an 11 at the last, a 106 that is the highest round the course has produced in 22 prior TEG visits (cr02, b46, b36) — and he still gives back only one point of the twelve, because nobody behind him does better; then R3 he wins outright again, 21 points across holes 11-16 (b04), and the lead is back to twelve. Resolution: R4 is his worst round of the week, 38 points with a 10 at the 14th and an 8 at the 17th (b25, b43), and it does not matter — the margin shrinks to eight and the Trophy is his, a second one to go with three Spoons.
headline_candidates: Baker Wins It on Day One

trophy_storyline.chosen_headline: Baker Wins It on Day One
trophy_storyline.standfirst: A 46 in the opening round put twelve points between Alex Baker and John Patterson; across the next three days the runner-up took back only four of them.

jacket_storyline.subject: Gregg Williams, reigning Wooden Spoon holder, improves in every round and turns a wretched R1 into the Green Jacket by fourteen
jacket_storyline.why_it_matters: Williams arrived as the man who finished last at TEG 17 and left with the Jacket at +66, the sixth-best gross total in TEG history, having got better every single day.
jacket_storyline.shape: Setup: R1 on the Tour is a shambles — a 9 at the 7th, an 8 at the 17th, eight shots bled across 3-5 (b24, b20) — 27 over par and third of five, with only a birdie at the 15th to stop the bleeding (b31). Turn: R2 he goes 14 over, four holes without dropping a gross shot across 13-16 and 13 points with them (b19, b26, b38, b42), drawing level with Jon Baker's gross lead and then taking it outright at the 2nd in R3 (b34, b28) after 12 points across holes 2-5 (b16, b21). Resolution: 13 and then 12 over on the Stadium, including a personal best 84 in the final round, nine points across 8-10 (b06, b10, b27, b12), and by the close he has both the Jacket by fourteen and, absurdly, closed to within nine of the Trophy lead he trailed by fifteen (b08, b02).
headline_candidates: Williams Improves Every Round, Wins By Fourteen

jacket_storyline.chosen_headline: Williams Improves Every Round, Wins By Fourteen
jacket_storyline.standfirst: Twenty-seven over par on Saturday and third of five; by Tuesday he had a personal-best 84 on the Stadium and the Green Jacket by a distance.

spoon_storyline.subject: Jon Baker arrives as defending Trophy and Jacket champion and leaves 23 points adrift at the bottom, last in three of the four rounds
spoon_storyline.why_it_matters: The reigning double champion took the Wooden Spoon, finished 43 points behind his own brother, and was last in the field in three of the four rounds — the steepest fall available in a five-man tournament.
spoon_storyline.shape: Setup: he holds the gross lead from the 5th in R1 for twenty holes, the longest tenure anyone manages all week, then loses it at the 7th in R2 and never gets it back (b48). Turn: R2 is his one good day — 39 points, 16 of them across the closing five holes without dropping a gross shot (b09, b13) — and it turns out to be a false dawn, because a 9 at the 4th in R3 (b39) drops him to the bottom of the Spoon race at the 2nd that same round and he stays there. Resolution: 28 and 29 points on the Stadium, 126 for the week, 23 behind David Mullin as the next worst (b14), while the Trophy goes to the brother who spent the last three TEGs collecting Spoons.

spoon_storyline.chosen_headline: Last Year's Double Winner Takes the Spoon
spoon_storyline.standfirst: Jon Baker landed in Girona holding both the Trophy and the Green Jacket, led the gross for twenty holes, and finished 43 points behind his own brother.

discovered_storylines.subject: David Mullin's week of extremes: an 11 in R1, the lowest gross round the Stadium has ever surrendered in R3, and nine shots gone in four holes in R4
discovered_storylines.why_it_matters: Mullin produced both the best single round in the Stadium course's TEG history and one of the week's worst holes, and finished with neither trophy to show for it.
discovered_storylines.shape: Setup: an 11 at the 15th in R1 on the Tour drops him straight to the bottom of the Wooden Spoon race (b35, b66) — a start with no obvious way back. Turn: on the Stadium in R3 he shoots 84 gross, breaking a course record of 89 that had stood across 27 prior visits and bettering his own mark there by seven (cr01). Resolution: R4 undoes it — four holes from the 14th without a net par, nine shots bled (b45, b49) — and he ends the week as Jacket runner-up, fourteen behind Williams (b02), holder of the best round ever played at the venue and nothing else.

discovered_storylines.standfirst: An 11 at the 15th on Saturday, the lowest gross round the Stadium has ever given up on Monday, and nine shots gone in four holes on Tuesday.

discovered_storylines.subject: John Patterson is bottom of the Wooden Spoon race after four holes of the tournament and finishes as Trophy runner-up, eight points back
discovered_storylines.why_it_matters: The man who bled 22 shots between the 3rd and the 10th on the opening morning ended up the only player who got anywhere near Alex Baker.
discovered_storylines.shape: Setup: an 8 at the 3rd in R1, seven holes without a net par, 22 shots dropped across 3-10, and bottom of the Spoon race by the 4th (b23, b18, b29, b33). Turn: the back nine of that same round is a different tournament — 13 points across 13-16 and a fourteen-point split between the nines (b30, b22) — and the pattern repeats in R2, where an 8 at the 4th and eleven shots gone across 6-10 are answered by 16 points across 11-15 (b15, b32, b11, b41). Resolution: he holds it together for a nine-point burst across 4-6 in R4 and a birdie at the 17th to end a run of bogeys or worse (b07, b03), finishing second on the Trophy, eight behind (b01) — the closest anyone came, from the worst possible start.

discovered_storylines.chosen_headline: Last After Four Holes, Second After Four Rounds
discovered_storylines.standfirst: John Patterson dropped 22 shots between the 3rd and the 10th on the opening day, and still finished the closest thing Alex Baker had to a rival.

vehicle_fit_response.note: The blow-ups are real — four from Alex Baker, three from Jon, plus a course-worst 106 — but they are texture inside the storylines rather than the shape of the report; the week's actual story is the two Bakers swapping ends of the table, and catalogue has framed two of the last three reports.

why_the_champion_won: It was settled on day one: Alex Baker's 46 in R1 put twelve points between him and John Patterson, and over the remaining three rounds Patterson took back only four of them — Baker won two rounds outright, never finished a round worse than third of five, and was the steadiest man in the field, so the margin he inherited from everyone else's opening day never had to be defended twice.
